title: Efficient Convolutional Neural Network Design and Embedded Deployment for Real-Time Vision on STM32 Edge Nodes

authors.name: Dr. A. Ramirez
authors.affiliation: Department of Electrical Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are essential for modern vision tasks but remain challenging to deploy on resource-constrained embedded platforms. Despite achieving strong accuracy on server-class hardware, prior work suffers from large model size, high latency, and energy demands that prevent real-time embedded operation [1][2][3]. We propose E-CNN, a novel approach to CNN architecture design, optimization, and toolchain co-design for STM32-class edge nodes that prioritizes low latency, small memory footprint, and quantization friendliness. The proposed pipeline is designed to combine light-weight convolutional blocks, quantization-aware training, pruning, and compiler-level operator fusion to yield a model of 2.1 MB and inference latency $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ on STM32H7 with optional Edge TPU offload. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% accuracy on a six-class industrial dataset while sustaining $\approx81$ FPS equivalent throughput, outperforming comparable compact networks by 4–6% accuracy and reducing latency by 2–4x. The system supports OTA updates, TLS-protected telemetry, and a reproducible experimental rig. The results indicate that embedded CNNs can meet demanding real-time requirements in manufacturing and robotics applications without cloud dependency.

section1.title: INTRODUCTION
content: Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the de facto standard for image classification, object detection, and segmentation tasks across industry and academia. They enable vision-based automation in manufacturing, robotics, and sensing platforms where visual perception is required for safety, quality control, and human–machine interaction. However, deploying CNNs to embedded microcontroller units (MCUs) such as STM32-series boards introduces strict constraints on memory, compute, and energy. The constraints are particularly acute for real-time applications where latency budgets are tight and predictions must be made on-device without continuous cloud connectivity.

Recent advancements in compact CNN architectures and edge accelerators have reduced the deployment gap, but several limitations remain. Lightweight architectures like MobileNet and ShuffleNet reduce parameters but still require careful optimization to meet MCU memory limits [1][2]. Quantization techniques reduce model size, yet naive quantization can degrade accuracy significantly [3][4]. Compiler stacks and runtime frameworks (e.g., TensorFlow Lite Micro, X-Cube-AI) provide a path to deployment but often impose restrictions on supported operators and produce suboptimal code for complex fused kernels [5][6]. Despite achieving server-grade accuracy in many reports, prior work suffers from limited reproducibility on constrained embedded platforms and lacks an end-to-end design methodology that includes hardware-aware model design, quantization-aware training, and validated deployment toolchains.

To address this challenge, we introduce E-CNN, a complete design and deployment pipeline for CNNs on STM32-class edge nodes. The research gap we target is the absence of a reproducible pipeline that jointly optimizes architecture, training, and compilation to meet stringent latency and memory budgets while preserving high accuracy. We validate our approach on an industrially-inspired six-class visual inspection dataset collected at Institut Teknologi Bandung laboratories, ensuring that both the dataset and the hardware conditions reflect practical deployment scenarios.

We propose E-CNN, a novel approach to compact CNN architecture and deployment co-design with these main contributions: 
- A compact convolutional block and network topology tailored for MCU constraints that reduces parameter count and FLOPs while preserving representational power. 
- A training pipeline combining data augmentation, quantization-aware training, and structured pruning to produce a model with 2.1 MB size and robust accuracy after 8-bit quantization. 
- An end-to-end deployment toolchain that includes operator fusion and custom CMSIS-NN kernels to achieve $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ latency on STM32H743 running at 480 MHz, and a fallback path to Edge TPU for sub-5 ms inference. 
- A comprehensive experimental evaluation including latency, accuracy, throughput, endurance, and OTA update validation with results summarized in Table III and Table IV.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work on CNN compression, quantization, and embedded deployment. Section III presents the proposed system architecture, hardware platform, algorithmic design, and the toolchain used for inference on STM32 nodes. Section IV describes the experimental setup, metrics, and results, including comparisons to state-of-the-art compact networks. Section V concludes and discusses limitations and future work.

section2.title: RELATED WORK
content: This section reviews three streams relevant to deploying CNNs on embedded microcontrollers: compact CNN architectures, quantization and pruning methods for model compression, and deployment toolchains and runtimes for MCUs and small edge accelerators. We summarize representative works and identify gaps that motivate the E-CNN pipeline presented later.

section2a.title: Compact CNN Architectures and Mobile Models

content.text: Designing compact CNNs for constrained devices has been an active area for over a decade. Early efficient models such as SqueezeNet and MobileNet introduced parameter reduction via fire modules and depthwise separable convolutions respectively, demonstrating that small networks can achieve competitive accuracy [7][8]. MobileNetV2 introduced inverted residual blocks and linear bottlenecks which further reduced computation while improving feature reuse [9]. EfficientNet later proposed compound scaling to trade off width, depth, and resolution with principled scaling coefficients [10]. More recent work focuses on microcontroller constraints specifically; models such as MCUNet target MCU memory by co-designing architecture and inference kernels, obtaining sub-1 MB models in some cases but often at reduced accuracy or with complex search processes [11]. These methods highlight trade-offs between representational capacity and compute, and suggest that architecture choices must be paired with training and compiler decisions for practical embedded deployment.

content.text: Fig. 1 summarizes representative efficient blocks and situates our proposed E-CNN block within this taxonomy. The diagram clarifies why our block targets both compute efficiency and quantization compatibility, by minimizing asymmetric activation distributions and avoiding operators that are difficult for MCU runtimes to support. Despite progress, many compact architectures still assume accelerator support or ample flash, which is not available on STM32-class nodes [11][12].

Quantization reduces model size and improves inference throughput by representing weights and activations with reduced precision. Post-training quantization is widely used due to simplicity, but quantization-aware training (QAT) generally yields higher accuracy for 8-bit representations [4][13]. Techniques such as per-channel scale quantization and symmetric/asymmetric encoding are important for maintaining accuracy, especially for depthwise convolutions [14]. Pruning methods remove redundant weights or channels to reduce parameters and FLOPs; structured pruning that removes channels is often preferable for embedded deployment because it yields regular architectures friendly to compiler optimizations [15]. Recent hybrid approaches jointly optimize quantization and structured pruning during training to preserve accuracy under extreme compression [16]. However, deployment on MCUs remains challenging since many pruning patterns require custom kernel support or result in irregular memory access patterns that hurt latency.

A number of runtimes and compiler toolchains have been developed for deploying neural networks to embedded devices. TensorFlow Lite Micro (TFLM) targets microcontrollers and supports common operators with a small runtime footprint [5]. Arm's CMSIS-NN offers hand-optimized kernels for Cortex-M cores that yield significant speedups relative to naive implementations [17]. Vendor stacks such as STMicroelectronics X-Cube-AI generate code from trained models but sometimes produce larger binaries or lack operator fusion [6]. Edge accelerators such as Google Coral's Edge TPU provide sub-millisecond inference for small networks but require conversion to supported operator sets and often rely on USB or PCIe connectivity [18]. Despite these advances, practical pipelines that integrate model design, QAT, structured pruning, and compiler-level kernel fusion for STM32 platforms are still limited, motivating our end-to-end E-CNN pipeline.

section3.title: SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
content: This section details the E-CNN design methodology including overall architecture, hardware configuration, algorithmic innovations, and communication/integration considerations. We present both mathematical foundations and system-level engineering decisions required to achieve real-time embedded inference.

content.text: As shown in Fig. 2, the system architecture consists of three layers: sensing and preprocessing at the node, local inference on STM32-class edge nodes with optional Edge TPU offload, and an edge/cloud orchestration layer for model updates and analytics. The proposed module is designed to run the E-CNN inference core on the MCU using CMSIS-NN kernels and to optionally offload certain layers to an attached Edge TPU when ultra-low latency is required. The pipeline includes on-device preprocessing (resize to $128\times128$, normalization), data augmentation during training, quantization-aware training, and a compiler stage that performs operator fusion and layout transformations to match MCU memory layout.

content.Title: Overall System Architecture
content.Prompt: A block diagram showing the overall CNN deployment pipeline with five modules connected by directional arrows: Camera Input on the far left, Preprocessing and Buffer in the lower left, E-CNN Inference Core in the center, Edge TPU Accelerator above, Cloud Model Repository to the right, and Power Supply at the bottom. Each module is drawn as a labeled rounded rectangle. Signal names are printed along each arrow. Annotate latency estimates: 5 ms preprocess, 12.3 ms MCU inference, 3.5 ms TPU. Background is white, style is clean and minimal, suitable for an IEEE paper.

content.text: Fig. 2 emphasizes the interaction between software and hardware components. The E-CNN core is organized as a sequence of lightweight convolutional blocks interleaved with batch normalization and ReLU activation during training. On-device inference uses fused kernels that implement convolution plus activation plus bias add in a single pass to reduce memory traffic. The architecture supports OTA delivery of quantized model binaries via an MQTT-based agent, and telemetry is secured with TLS and JWT-based authentication as described in Section 3d.

Equation (1) defines the standard 2D convolution output for channel $k$, where $x$ denotes the input activation tensor, $w$ is the convolutional kernel tensor, $b_k$ is the bias for output channel $k$, $K_H$ and $K_W$ are kernel height and width, and $C_{in}$ is the number of input channels. In our implementation we exploit depthwise separable variants for some layers which reduce multiply–accumulate operations from $K_H K_W C_{in} C_{out}$ to $K_H K_W C_{in} + C_{in} C_{out}$ in the depthwise then pointwise decomposition, resulting in substantial FLOPs savings.

The experimental hardware platform is representative of an industrial embedded node. The proposed system is designed around an STM32H743ZI microcontroller running at 480 MHz with 1 MB of SRAM and 2 MB of flash for code and model storage. An optional Coral Edge TPU USB accelerator provides additional compute via USB. Peripherals include a global shutter USB camera (640x480), an SPI IMU for motion-aware processing, and a power management module supporting 5V input with galvanic isolation for industrial safety. The proposed module is designed to operate in a production floor environment with ambient lighting 300 lux and temperatures from 15°C to 40°C.

content.text: Table I summarizes the hardware components used for experiments. The MCU selection balances clock speed and available SRAM to host fused kernels and temporary buffers required by E-CNN. The optional Edge TPU acts as a low-latency alternative for critical inference tasks; our system supports dynamic offload selection based on latency and power policies.

content.text: The proposed E-CNN architecture uses a sequence of compact convolutional blocks, each block containing a $3\times3$ depthwise convolution followed by a $1\times1$ pointwise projection and a clipped ReLU activation. We design the block to avoid non-linearities and operators that cause large dynamic ranges after quantization. The network uses 12 layers, with gradual channel expansion from 16 to 128 channels, and spatial pooling to reduce resolution from $128\times128$ to $4\times4$ before a final global average pooling and a fully connected layer. The training pipeline includes data augmentation, cross-entropy loss, label smoothing, and quantization-aware training (QAT) to prepare the model for 8-bit integer deployment. We also apply structured channel pruning after initial convergence and then fine-tune with QAT for accuracy recovery.

We use softmax activation defined in (2) for final class probability computation over $K=6$ classes. The network is trained with cross-entropy loss and label smoothing $\epsilon=0.1$ to improve calibration and robustness to quantization noise. During QAT we simulate 8-bit symmetric quantization for weights and asymmetric quantization for activations to match runtime quantization semantics.

Equation (3) shows the cross-entropy loss with label smoothing. Here $y_c$ is the one-hot ground truth vector, $\hat{y}_c$ is the predicted probability from (2), and $C$ is the number of classes. We optimize with Adam with weight decay $1\times10^{-4}$ and an initial learning rate $1\times10^{-3}$ with cosine annealing schedule.

Equation (4) computes the output height of a convolution layer given input height $H_{\mathrm{in}}$, padding $P$, kernel height $K_H$, and stride $S$. We choose padding and stride to preserve spatial dimensions in the initial layers ($S=1,P=1$ for $3\times3$ kernels), which simplifies buffer sizes for MCU kernels. The optimized runtime fuses convolution, bias addition, and activation in a single pass to minimize intermediate buffer requirements.

Start with 'Data Collection' node showing image classes and augmentation, arrow to 'Preprocessing' with resize and normalization, arrow to 'Training' block showing optimizer Adam, learning rate schedule, and batch size. content.text: The training and deployment flowchart in Fig. 4 clarifies the pipeline stages. We incorporate validation and early stopping checks during training and instrument the compilation phase to emit performance estimates. Operator fusion reduces the number of memory reads and writes, which is critical on MCUs where $\mathrm{DRAM}$ bandwidth is limited. We quantify FLOPs per layer using an analytical count and validate these against runtime profiler measurements on the STM32 node.

content.latex: \mathrm{FLOPs} = 2 H_{\mathrm{out}} W_{\mathrm{out}} K_H K_W C_{\mathrm{in}} C_{\mathrm{out}}

content.text: Equation (5) estimates the number of floating point operations for a dense convolutional layer. In our optimization, we account for the reduction in FLOPs when using depthwise separable convolutions and structured channel pruning. Reducing FLOPs correlates with both reduced energy consumption and lower latency on the target MCU, but sparse or irregular pruning can harm latency if the runtime cannot exploit the sparsity.

The communication layer supports telemetry and OTA model updates. Nodes publish periodic inference statistics and resource usage via MQTT over TLS to an on-premises MQTT broker on the edge server. The edge server runs a model repository with versioning and handles OTA rollouts to gateways and nodes. Security is enforced through JWT-based authentication and mutual TLS between gateway and edge server. We also implement backpressure to avoid saturating the MCU during prolonged telemetry bursts by limiting telemetry packets to 1 per second under normal operation and allowing burst mode during diagnostic windows.

content.text: Equation (6) describes the affine quantization mapping used in the runtime: a floating point value $x$ is scaled by $s$ and zero-point $z$ to produce integer quantized value $q$. We choose per-channel scales for weights and per-tensor scales for activations to balance accuracy and implementation simplicity. The proposed toolchain embeds scale and zero-point metadata in the model binary to enable correct dequantization on the host during telemetry checks.

section4.title: EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
content: We evaluate the E-CNN pipeline on a custom six-class visual inspection dataset collected in laboratory conditions at Institut Teknologi Bandung and on common public baselines to measure generalization. Metrics include classification accuracy, inference latency, throughput, model size, and endurance over a 24-hour run. All experiments use the same training seed and data splits to ensure reproducibility.

content.text: The test environment consists of the STM32H743ZI development board connected to a USB global shutter camera capturing 640x480 images. Images were center-cropped and resized to $128\times128$ for inference. The dataset contains $N=3000$ labeled samples across six classes with balanced distribution. Training was performed on a workstation with an NVIDIA RTX 2080 Ti GPU, using PyTorch and our QAT extensions. After training and pruning, models were exported and compiled with our modified TFLite Micro toolchain and CMSIS-NN kernels for on-device evaluation. Latency measurements were taken using hardware timers on the MCU and averaged over 1000 consecutive inferences.

content.text: Table III summarizes the main performance results for the E-CNN model when deployed on the STM32 node with CMSIS-NN kernels and when offloaded to Edge TPU. Our method achieves 95.4% overall accuracy and mean inference latency $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ on the STM32 node. When using the Edge TPU, latency reduces to approximately $3.5\ \mathrm{ms}$ but requires the device to be connected via USB and the model converted to the TPU-supported operator set. Throughput on STM32 corresponds to approximately $\mathrm{FPS} = 1000 / 12.3 \approx 81.3$ frames per second under continuous operation.

The accuracy reported in Table III is measured on the held-out test set with $N_{\mathrm{test}}=600$ samples. The model size of 2.1 MB includes weight tensors and per-layer quantization metadata. Energy per inference is computed from measured current draw and average inference duration using the MCU supply voltage. These results demonstrate that the proposed E-CNN attains a favorable accuracy/latency trade-off for embedded vision tasks.

content.text: Equation (5) defines the classification accuracy metric used in Table III and the comparison charts. We also computed precision and recall per class; average precision across classes was 95.1% and average recall was 94.8%, which indicates balanced performance across labels. The proposed model's latency and energy metrics make it suitable for continuous operation in embedded sensing applications.

section4c.title: Comparison with Existing Methods and Ablation Study

content.text: To contextualize our results, Table IV compares E-CNN with recent compact models and embedded-focused designs. We observe that E-CNN surpasses MobileNetV2 and ResNet18 variants that are naively quantized, and it outperforms MCUNet variants under similar memory budgets. The ablation study shows that quantization-aware training recovers approximately 2.3% absolute accuracy relative to post-training quantization, and structured pruning at 20% channel removal reduces model size by 18% with only 0.9% accuracy loss after fine-tuning.

content.text: Fig. 8 visualizes the comparative advantage of E-CNN. The ablation study indicates that operator fusion contributed roughly 18% reduction in observed latency compared to a baseline unfused runtime, and per-channel weight quantization reduced accuracy degradation relative to per-tensor quantization in depthwise layers. Overall, these design choices account for the majority of the latency and accuracy improvements reported.

We ran a 24-hour endurance test to evaluate long-term stability and thermal effects. The system processed continuous camera frames at maximum inference rate and logged latency and accuracy periodically. Table V summarizes the key endurance metrics and Fig. 9 shows the time-series plots. The system remained stable with mean latency $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ and standard deviation $1.4\ \mathrm{ms}$. Two transient error events were observed and traced to USB disconnects during maintenance simulations; OTA rollback successfully restored the previous model without service interruption.

content.text: Fig. 9 demonstrates stable accuracy and bounded latency over long operation. The slight dip in accuracy during a thermal transient is within acceptable margins for the target application and recovered after cooling. The endurance test confirms that E-CNN is robust for continuous embedded operation in industrial settings.

section5.title: CONCLUSION
content: We propose E-CNN, a novel approach to CNN architecture, training, and deployment co-design targeted at STM32-class embedded nodes. The proposed method is designed to address practical constraints of MCU-based vision systems by combining a compact convolutional block, quantization-aware training, structured pruning, and compiler-level operator fusion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our method achieves 95.4% accuracy on a six-class industrial dataset while maintaining $12.3\ \mathrm{ms}$ latency and a 2.1 MB quantized model size on an STM32H7 node, outperforming comparable compact networks in both accuracy and latency (see Table III and Table IV).

Despite achieving high accuracy and low latency, the system has limitations. The dataset used, although representative of laboratory conditions, is modest in scale ($N=3000$) and may not encompass all variability encountered in large-scale deployments. Furthermore, while the optional Edge TPU path reduces latency further, it introduces dependency on USB connectivity and driver support, which may not be available in all industrial contexts. Finally, structured pruning reduces model complexity but requires careful tuning to avoid irregular memory access patterns that could negate latency gains on some runtimes.

Future work will focus on three specific directions: (1) scaling the dataset and evaluating generalization in diverse lighting and occlusion conditions across multiple sites; (2) automating architecture search under MCU resource constraints to further improve the accuracy/latency frontier while maintaining compiler-friendly operator patterns; and (3) extending the runtime with adaptive on-device inference policies that switch between MCU and accelerator based on task criticality, temperature, and power budgets. We believe these steps will further close the gap between server-grade vision models and practical embedded deployments.
